newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC accused of ignoring human rights.
newsitem.headline: APEC accused of ignoring human rights.

text.p: Asia-Pacific nations may be marching towards ever greater prosperity but are trampling all over human rights, especially those of the poor, women and migrant workers, Amnesty International said on Saturday.
"If APEC means business, then human rights should be APEC's business," Ross Daniels, executive committee member of the London-based rights group, told a Manila news conference.
"APEC means business" is one of the slogans plastered all over the Philippine capital as it hosts the annual gathering of the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, China's Jiang Zemin, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and their colleagues were among leaders flying in on Saturday for their fourth annual summit, to be held at Subic Bay north of Manila on Monday.
Their goal is to turn the region into the world's biggest free trade zone accounting for more than half its population and industrial output.
But Amnesty was concerned human rights was not on their agenda.
"We're for APEC if it brings about justice and greater prosperity for people... but we're against it if there's a whole lot of evils associated with it," Daniels said.
Despite considerable economic progress, human rights abuses in China and Indonesia had become substantially worse, the Australian activist said.
In China, workers in boom areas were being ruthlessly exploited and the Indonesian government was increasingly intolerant of the slightest sign of criticism, he said.
Women, migrant workers and the poor bore the brunt of the abuse, Amnesty said.

"Economic liberalisation and growth have deepened the marginalisation of the poor and vulnerable groups and contributed to further violations of their human rights," the rights group said in a report.

There has been strong pressure within APEC, particularly from the United States, to try to get it to broaden its focus to include human rights and environmental concerns, diplomats and APEC officials said.

But this has met strong resistance, especially from southeast Asian nations such as Singapore and Malaysia who have long insisted that western ideas about rights should not be imposed on Asia, which has its own values.
Amnesty gave a qualified welcome to a pledge by Philippine President Fidel Ramos, the summit host, to push for a greater involvement by rights groups in APEC's deliberations.
"If it happens... it may go some way to ensuring APEC no longer has such a narrow agenda," Daniels said.
He said Amnesty had had little success in interesting the private sector, which is being given a higher profile than ever at the Philippine summit, in rights issues.
"Every time you talk to a business person they say this is not about human rights," Daniels said.

Amnesty officials expressed concern at the tight security restrictions in the Philippines surrounding the summit and said they hoped a protest caravan due to travel north from Manila to the summit venue at Subic Bay would not be harassed.
"We will be very concerned indeed if there is any heavy-handed crackdown," Daniels said.
